triggers: how do I check disk space
how do I see how much disk space I have
what command shows disk usage
how do I check free disk space
how can I see how full my disk is
what's the command to check storage
answer:
Check disk space with `df`:

```
df -h            # free/used space per filesystem, human-readable
df -h /          # just the root filesystem
du -sh <dir>     # how much a particular folder is using
du -sh * | sort -h   # biggest items in the current directory
```

`df` shows whole filesystems; `du` measures specific paths. For a graphical view, open **Disk Usage Analyzer**.

answer:
Check memory with `free`:

```
free -h          # total / used / free RAM and swap, human-readable
free -h -s 2     # refresh every 2 seconds
```

For a live, per-process view use `top` (or `htop` where installed) and look at the RES column.

answer:
Show the running kernel with `uname`:

```
uname -r         # kernel release, e.g. 6.18.10-igos-2
uname -a         # full: kernel, hostname, arch, build date
```

`uname -r` is the one most tools want.

answer:
Show how long the machine has been up with `uptime`:

```
uptime           # current time, uptime, users, load averages
uptime -p        # 'pretty' form, e.g. 'up 3 hours, 12 minutes'
```

For when it last booted: `uptime -s`.

answer:
List running processes with `ps`, or watch them live:

```
ps aux               # every process, with CPU and memory
ps aux | grep <name> # find a specific one
top                  # live, sorted by CPU (q to quit)
htop                 # friendlier live view, where installed
```

To stop one, note its PID and `kill <pid>`.

triggers: how do I find large files
answer:
```
du -ah ~ | sort -rh | head -20         # 20 biggest files+dirs under your home
```
For a whole filesystem: `sudo du -ahx / | sort -rh | head -20`. The interactive TUI tool
**ncdu** is handy if installed (`sudo pkm install ncdu`).

triggers: how do I free up disk space
answer:
Three safe reclaim steps on InterGenOS:
```
sudo pkm autoremove          # drop orphaned dependency packages
sudo pkm cache clean         # prune old cached package archives (keeps current)
journalctl --disk-usage      # see how much the system logs use
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M   # cap the journal
```
Then find big user files with `du -ah ~ | sort -rh | head -20`.

triggers: how do I free up memory
how do I free up my memory

free up memory
how do I free up RAM
free up RAM
how do I reduce memory usage
how do I clear memory
answer:
On Linux, high memory "used" usually isn't something to fix. The kernel deliberately uses spare RAM for disk cache, and it hands that memory straight back the moment an app needs it — so `free -h` showing little **free** is normal and healthy. Read the **available** column, not **free**:
```
free -h                      # total / used / available RAM and swap
top                          # live view — press Shift+M to sort by memory
```
If the machine actually feels slow or an app is being starved, free memory the safe, user-driven way:
- **Close what you're not using** — browser tabs are the usual memory hog.
- Open **System Monitor -> Processes**, sort by Memory, and quit or restart a runaway process.
- **Reboot** if something has leaked and won't let go.

There's no command that safely "frees RAM" on its own — force-dropping caches just makes the next disk read slower. Adding physical RAM is a hardware change, not something software does.

triggers: how do I clean up my system
answer:
```
sudo pkm autoremove          # remove orphaned dependencies
sudo pkm cache clean         # prune downloaded package archives (--all wipes them all)
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M   # trim systemd journals
```
pkm has no equivalent of `apt autoclean` beyond `pkm cache clean`; that's the one to use.

triggers: how do I clear the package cache
answer:
```
sudo pkm cache clean          # keep the archive for each installed version, drop the rest
sudo pkm cache clean --all    # remove every cached archive (re-downloaded on next install)
sudo pkm cache clean --rollback   # prune the pre-upgrade rollback snapshots too
```
The cache lives at `/var/cache/pkm/`. `clean` (default) is safe; `--all` frees the most.

triggers: how do I change my computer's name
how do I rename this computer
how do I change the hostname
how do I set the machine name
change my computer name
answer:
The computer's name (its hostname) is set with **`hostnamectl`**:
```
hostnamectl                              # show the current hostname
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname <new-name>   # set a new one
```
Use a short name with letters, digits, and hyphens (no spaces). The change takes effect immediately — open a new terminal to see it in your prompt. You can also change it from **Settings → About → Device Name**.

This is **InterGenOS**, a from-source Linux distribution. The exact release is recorded in `/etc/os-release`:
```
cat /etc/os-release    # NAME, VERSION, and the release id
```
For the running kernel specifically, `uname -r`. (`lsb_release -a` prints the same distribution fields in a compact form.)

triggers: what disks do I have
show my drives
list my partitions
what drives are connected
what storage devices are there
show my disks
answer:
InterGenOS lists the block devices (disks and their partitions) with:
```
lsblk                  # tree of disks, partitions, sizes, and mountpoints
```
Each top-level entry (`sda`, `nvme0n1`, ...) is a physical disk; the indented rows beneath it are its partitions. To see how full a mounted filesystem is, use `df -h`; to see filesystem types, `lsblk -f`.

answer:
The computer's name (its hostname) is shown by:
```
hostnamectl            # current hostname plus OS / kernel / hardware summary
```

The first line, **Static hostname**, is the machine's name. To *change* it, `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname <new-name>`.
